items.scenario: You ask Claude to summarise a 40-message migration thread into a paragraph plus an action table. The table lists 'Owner: Ravi, Due: Friday' for a DNS cutover. You don't remember Ravi agreeing to anything.
items.question: What is the most likely explanation and the right next step?
options: Claude must have seen a message you missed — post the table as is
The table format invited the model to fill empty Owner/Due cells with plausible values; check the source message and mark it UNASSIGNED / NO DATE if nobody committed
Ravi is the most senior engineer, so the assignment is reasonable — keep it
Re-run the same prompt until the owner changes, then pick the most common answer
items.explanation: Hallucinated owners and dates are a known summarisation failure: structured formats pressure the model to fill every cell. Require a source citation per action and verify against the thread.
distractors: Possible, but unverified. Posting an unchecked attribution assigns work to someone who never agreed.
Plausibility isn't agreement. Inferring owners is exactly the error to avoid.
Re-sampling measures consistency, not truth. The source thread is the only authority.

items.scenario: During a SEV-2 checkout outage you need a public status-page update and an exec update. You have confirmed impact, start time and current mitigation, but no root cause yet.
items.question: How should you use Claude?
options: Ask Claude to write one update that works for everyone, including a likely root cause to reassure customers
Give Claude only confirmed facts and ask for two registers: customer-facing (impact, mitigation, next update time, no speculation) and exec (impact, ETA confidence, decision needed)
Paste the full internal incident channel so Claude can decide what's public
Wait until the root cause is known before using Claude for any communication
items.explanation: Same facts, different readers: register is chosen deliberately. Confirmed facts only — public speculation about root cause has to be retracted later.
distractors: One-size-fits-all fails both readers, and a speculative root cause on a public page is a commitment you can't back.
Over-sharing internal context (names, speculation, possibly customer data) and delegating the public/private judgment to the model.
Stakeholder updates are needed during the incident; Claude speeds them up as long as you supply only verified facts.

items.scenario: Your weekly client status email, drafted by Claude from stand-up notes, contains: 'The reporting export will ship next sprint.' Internally this was only a stretch goal.
items.question: Which part of sending discipline catches this?
options: Checking the email's tone
Checking every commitment — anything that reads as a promise must have been agreed by someone with authority
Running a spell check
Checking the subject line is under 60 characters
items.explanation: Read before send means checking every name, number and commitment. Drafting models turn tentative internal language into confident statements.
distractors: Tone can be perfect while the content makes an unauthorised promise.
Spelling is correct here; the problem is meaning, not orthography.
Formatting rules don't catch content errors.

items.scenario: You need a 12-page runbook for a new service. A colleague suggests asking Claude to 'write the full runbook' in one prompt to save time.
items.question: Which approach produces the most reliable document?
options: One prompt for the whole runbook, then a single read-through
Outline first (sections with purpose and reader takeaway), approve it, generate section by section, then run a consistency and glossary pass
Ask Claude to write it three times and merge the best paragraphs
Write it yourself — Claude can't handle long documents
items.explanation: Outline-first fixes the argument cheaply, section-level generation limits drift, and consistency/glossary passes catch contradictions in terms and numbers.
distractors: Long one-shot output drifts and is hard to review thoroughly.
Merging three drafts multiplies inconsistency rather than removing it.
Over-correction: long documents work well with the structured approach.

items.scenario: An approved design doc must go to the CTO and to the team implementing it.
items.question: What's the best way to adapt it?
options: Send the same doc to both and ask Claude to make it 'more professional'
Create an exec version leading with decision, cost, risk and timeline, and an engineering version with interfaces, migration and rollback — same facts, different reader
Shorten the doc by 50% and send that to both
Translate the technical terms into simpler words for both audiences
items.explanation: Rewriting for a defined reader beats generic 'improve it' requests. Register is a choice: execs need the decision first; engineers need the detail.
distractors: 'More professional' is vague and doesn't serve either reader's needs.
Uniform cutting removes what each audience needs.
Engineers need the precise terms; simplifying them for the implementers loses information.

items.scenario: A draft proposal has good sentences but the argument is in the wrong order and a cost section is missing. A teammate has started line-editing it with Claude.
items.question: What should happen first?
options: Continue line edits, then fix structure at the end
Ask Claude for a structural critique without rewriting — order, gaps, what to cut — fix structure, then line-edit
Run a grammar check, then send
Ask Claude to rewrite the whole proposal from scratch
items.explanation: Structural edits come before line edits; polishing paragraphs that will be moved or deleted wastes effort.
distractors: Polished sentences may be cut when the structure changes — wasted work.
Grammar isn't the problem; the argument and the missing section are.
A from-scratch rewrite discards the good material and the author's intent without diagnosing the problem.

items.scenario: Your team writes many client emails and wants them to sound consistent: same product names, sign-off, banned phrases and glossary.
items.question: What's the most durable way to achieve this with Claude?
options: Each person types the rules into every chat when they remember
Put the team voice guide and glossary in a shared Project's instructions so every chat there starts with them
Ask Claude to remember the rules in one chat
Write one perfect email and have everyone copy it
items.explanation: Persistent instructions apply to every turn without anyone remembering to add them; in-context conditioning on house rules gives consistency.
distractors: Relying on memory means rules get forgotten or applied inconsistently.
One chat's context doesn't carry to the team's other chats.
A template covers one case; a voice guide generalises.

items.scenario: You ask Claude to summarise a private incident-review DM thread (it names a customer and an engineer's mistake) and post it in a public #engineering channel.
items.question: What is the main problem?
options: Summaries are usually too long for Slack
Posting a private conversation's summary in a public channel is a disclosure — check the audience before anything is posted
Claude can't summarise DMs
The summary should have used bullet points
items.explanation: Visibility and etiquette: assume everyone in the channel sees what's posted. Privacy rules from M8.1 apply to summaries as much as to originals.
distractors: Length is a style issue; the audience mismatch is the real problem.
Capability isn't the issue; whether you should is.
Formatting doesn't fix a disclosure.

items.scenario: Claude produces release notes from 60 commits. They read beautifully. Your reviewer approves them after a quick skim, and the notes describe an internal refactor as a new user-facing feature.
items.question: Which practice would most reliably have prevented this?
options: Asking for more polished wording
Requiring a commit hash citation for every line and verifying user-facing and breaking items against the diff, as a separate pass from reading for flow
Using a larger model
Having the reviewer read the notes twice
items.explanation: Fluent ≠ correct: polished text lowers vigilance. Traceability (citations) plus a deliberate verification pass catches mis-categorised changes.
distractors: Polish is what lulled the reviewer; more of it makes the problem worse.
Better models reduce errors but don't remove the need to verify.
Re-reading for flow repeats the same blind spot; verification needs a different method.

items.scenario: You correspond in English with a Japanese client about a contract change. You draft in English and want to send in Japanese.
items.question: What's the safest workflow?
options: Ask Claude for a Japanese version and send it directly — modern translation is accurate
Ask for the Japanese version in the right business register plus a back-translation to English, check meaning, and have a fluent colleague review anything with contractual weight
Send in English only; never use translation for clients
Send both the Japanese and the English versions without review so the client can compare
items.explanation: Multi-language drafting is a strength, but contractual and commercial terms need human verification. A back-translation exposes meaning drift you can check yourself.
distractors: Register, honorifics and legal terms are exactly where unchecked translation fails.
Over-correction: translation is valuable with the right checks.
Sending unreviewed text in two languages creates two unverified versions that may disagree.
